title: Health and the body
objectives: I can name the main parts of the body and explain why each word is spelled and stressed as it is.
I can say where it hurts and describe symptoms with doer and estar com, and say how long with desde and há.
I can give and understand advice with precisar, ter que, dever and the imperative, and tell them apart in the negative.
I can explain why Portuguese uses the article where English uses 'my' with body parts, and use reflexive verbs correctly.
I can talk about health care in Brazil: the SUS, plano de saúde and the pharmacy.

vocabulary.note: The cedilla writes the s sound before a: ca-BE-sa. Stress is on the second to last syllable, as the ending a predicts, so no accent is needed.

example.pt: A minha cabeça está doendo desde ontem.
example.en: My head has been hurting since yesterday.
example.literal: The my head is hurting since yesterday.

vocabulary.note: Plural: os olhos. The lh is one sound, like the lli of million. The vowel changes at the plural: the singular has a closed o (O-lyu) and the plural an open o (Ó-lyus). Spelling does not show this, so learn it with the word.

example.pt: Meus olhos estão vermelhos e doem.
example.en: My eyes are red and they hurt.

vocabulary.note: Built on ouvir, to hear, so it is the ear as the organ of hearing and the inner ear; dor de ouvido is an earache. The ou is a diphthong, one syllable: ou-VI-do. The visible outer ear is a orelha.

example.pt: Estou com dor de ouvido.
example.en: I have an earache.
example.literal: I-am with pain of ear.

vocabulary.note: The lh is one sound: o-RE-lha. Also used for the ears of animals and for the visible part of the ear where you wear earrings.

example.pt: Ela usa um brinco em cada orelha.
example.en: She wears an earring in each ear.
example.literal: She uses an earring in each ear.

vocabulary.note: Ends in z, so the default puts the stress on the last syllable (na-RIZ) and no accent is needed. Plural: os narizes, with the stress on the same syllable.

example.pt: Estou com o nariz entupido.
example.en: I have a stuffy nose.
example.literal: I-am with the nose stuffed.

vocabulary.note: The c before a is the k sound: BO-ka.

example.pt: Abra a boca e diga ah.
example.en: Open your mouth and say ah.
example.literal: Open the mouth and say ah.

vocabulary.note: The en is nasal, and the final e is said i, so the t before it is said ch: DEN-chi.

example.pt: Estou com dor de dente desde segunda.
example.en: I have had a toothache since Monday.
example.literal: I-am with pain of tooth since second.

vocabulary.note: Both g letters come before a, so both are the hard g. The an is nasal. The r closes the first syllable, so its sound depends on the region.

example.pt: Minha garganta está muito vermelha.
example.en: My throat is very red.

vocabulary.note: Two different letters in one word: the c before o is k and the ç before o is s, so it is said pes-KO-su. The sc here is not the digraph of nascer, because that reading only happens before e or i.

example.pt: Dormi mal e acordei com dor no pescoço.
example.en: I slept badly and woke up with a sore neck.
example.literal: I-slept badly and I-woke with pain in-the neck.

vocabulary.note: The ç before o is the s sound. The r after b is the quick tap.

example.pt: Ele quebrou o braço jogando futebol.
example.en: He broke his arm playing soccer.
example.literal: He broke the arm playing football.

vocabulary.note: Feminine although it ends in o, one of the exceptions to the gender endings. The tilde makes the vowel nasal and marks the stress: one syllable, said like ow through the nose. Plural: as mãos.

example.pt: Lave as mãos antes de comer.
example.en: Wash your hands before eating.
example.literal: Wash the hands before of to-eat.

vocabulary.note: Dedo da mão is finger and dedo do pé is toe. Said DE-du, with a closed e.

example.pt: Cortei o dedo cozinhando.
example.en: I cut my finger cooking.
example.literal: I-cut the finger cooking.

vocabulary.note: The r closes the first syllable, so its sound depends on the region: COR-pu.

example.pt: Estou com dor no corpo todo.
example.en: My whole body aches.
example.literal: I-am with pain in-the body whole.

vocabulary.note: The ei is a diphthong, one syllable: PEI-tu.

example.pt: Estou com dor no peito e falta de ar.
example.en: I have chest pain and shortness of breath.
example.literal: I-am with pain in-the chest and lack of air.

vocabulary.note: Always plural, even for one person's back: as costas, with the plural article. The o is open.

example.pt: Tenho dor nas costas por causa da cadeira.
example.en: I have back pain because of the chair.
example.literal: I-have pain in-the backs for cause of-the chair.

vocabulary.note: In everyday speech barriga is the stomach region, where English says stomach. The organ itself is o estômago. The rr is the strong r: ba-RRI-ga.

example.pt: Estou com dor de barriga desde o almoço.
example.en: I have had a stomachache since lunch.
example.literal: I-am with pain of belly since the lunch.

vocabulary.note: The r closes the first syllable: PER-na.

example.pt: Minhas pernas estão cansadas depois da corrida.
example.en: My legs are tired after the run.

vocabulary.note: Three syllables: jo-E-lho. The oe is two syllables because two strong vowels never glide together, and the stress is second to last as the ending o predicts, so no accent. The j is the zh sound and the lh is one sound.

example.pt: Dói o joelho quando eu subo a escada.
example.en: My knee hurts when I climb the stairs.
example.literal: Hurts the knee when I go-up the staircase.

vocabulary.note: Plural: os pés. A stressed one-syllable word ending in e carries an accent, and the acute shows the open e.

example.pt: Doem os meus pés depois de andar o dia todo.
example.en: My feet hurt after walking all day.
example.literal: Hurt the my feet after of to-walk the day whole.

vocabulary.note: Used almost only in the third person, because the subject is the body part that hurts: dói for one thing and doem for more than one. The acute on dói marks the open o of the stressed diphthong ói.

example.pt: Onde dói?
example.en: Where does it hurt?
example.literal: Where hurts?

vocabulary.note: Feminine although it ends in -or, like a flor and a cor. Ends in r, so the stress is on the last syllable. Plural: as dores, with the stress on the same syllable.

example.pt: Estou com muita dor nas costas.
example.en: I am in a lot of back pain.
example.literal: I-am with much pain in-the backs.

vocabulary.note: The e of the stressed syllable is open, which the spelling does not show. The final e is said i: FÉ-bri.

example.pt: Estou com febre desde ontem à noite.
example.en: I have had a fever since last night.
example.literal: I-am with fever since yesterday at-the night.

vocabulary.note: The ss between vowels writes the s sound; a single s there would be z. Said TÓ-si.

example.pt: Minha tosse não passa.
example.en: My cough will not go away.
example.literal: My cough not passes.

vocabulary.note: The g before r is the hard g. Brazilians say estar gripado for having a cold or flu (the ending -ado makes an adjective from the noun) and resfriado for a lighter cold, from resfriar, to catch a chill, which is built on frio, cold. Fiquei de cama means I stayed in bed.

example.pt: Fiquei de cama uma semana com a gripe.
example.en: I was in bed for a week with the flu.
example.literal: I-stayed of bed one week with the flu.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the third to last syllable, so the accent is required: re-MÉ-di-o. The open e takes the acute, and d before the i sound is said j. The verb for taking medicine is tomar, which also means to drink.

example.pt: Você já tomou o remédio?
example.en: Have you taken the medicine yet?
example.literal: You already took the medicine?

vocabulary.note: From comprimir, to compress: a pill is a compressed tablet. The m before p only nasalizes the vowel: com-pri-MI-do.

example.pt: Tome um comprimido de oito em oito horas.
example.en: Take one pill every eight hours.
example.literal: Take a pill of eight in eight hours.

vocabulary.note: Also the word for a cooking recipe. The c before e is s and the ei is a diphthong: re-CEI-ta.

example.pt: Esse remédio precisa de receita.
example.en: This medicine needs a prescription.
example.literal: This medicine needs of prescription.

vocabulary.note: Feminine: a médica. Stressed on the third to last syllable, so the accent is required: MÉ-di-co, with d said j. You address a doctor as doutor or doutora.

example.pt: A médica me examinou com muita atenção.
example.en: The doctor examined me very carefully.
example.literal: The doctor me examined with much attention.

vocabulary.note: The l that closes the first syllable is said w: con-SUW-ta. Marcar uma consulta is to book an appointment, literally to mark one; marquei has qu because c before e would be the s sound.

example.pt: Marquei uma consulta pra quinta-feira.
example.en: I booked an appointment for Thursday.
example.literal: I-marked an appointment for Thursday.

vocabulary.note: The document from a doctor that excuses you from work or school. Built on atestar, to certify.

example.pt: O médico me deu um atestado de dois dias.
example.en: The doctor gave me a two-day note.
example.literal: The doctor me gave a certificate of two days.

vocabulary.note: Three syllables: sa-Ú-de. The acute shows that the u is its own syllable; without it au would be one syllable, as in aula. People also say Saúde! after a sneeze and when raising a glass.

example.pt: A saúde é muito importante.
example.en: Health is very important.
example.literal: The health is very important.

example.pt: Meu plano de saúde cobre consultas.
example.en: My health insurance covers appointments.

vocabulary.note: Short for Sistema Único de Saúde, and said as a word: sus. Único is stressed on the third to last syllable, so it carries an accent. The system is free and open to everyone.

example.pt: No SUS eu não pago nada.
example.en: In the SUS I pay nothing.
example.literal: In-the SUS I not pay nothing.

example.pt: Fui ao posto de saúde hoje cedo.
example.en: I went to the health clinic early this morning.
example.literal: I-went to-the post of health today early.

vocabulary.note: A hyphenated compound: pronto is ready and socorro is aid, and Socorro! alone is the cry for help. The rr is the strong r: so-COR-ru.

example.pt: Ele foi ao pronto-socorro de madrugada.
example.en: He went to the emergency room in the early hours.
example.literal: He went to-the ready-aid of dawn.

vocabulary.note: From des-, which undoes, plus cansar, to tire. The s and the c before a are separate sounds: des-kan-SAR.

example.pt: Você precisa descansar mais.
example.en: You need to rest more.

dialogues.title: At the doctor
dialogues.context: Paulo visits Dr. Márcia with a sore throat and a fever.

lines.speaker: Márcia
lines.pt: Bom dia, Paulo. O que você está sentindo?
lines.en: Good morning, Paulo. What are you feeling?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Bom dia, doutora. Estou com dor de garganta e tosse há três dias.
lines.en: Good morning, doctor. I have had a sore throat and a cough for three days.
lines.literal: Good day, doctor. I-am with pain of throat and cough has three days.

lines.speaker: Márcia
lines.pt: Você está com febre?
lines.en: Do you have a fever?
lines.literal: You are with fever?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Estou. Ontem à noite deu trinta e oito graus.
lines.en: I do. Last night it reached thirty-eight degrees.
lines.literal: I-am. Yesterday at-the night gave thirty and eight degrees.

lines.speaker: Márcia
lines.pt: Onde dói mais? A garganta ou o peito?
lines.en: Where does it hurt more? The throat or the chest?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Dói mais a garganta. Também estou com dor no corpo.
lines.en: The throat hurts more. I also have body aches.
lines.literal: Hurts more the throat. Also I-am with pain in-the body.

lines.speaker: Márcia
lines.pt: Abra a boca e diga ah. A garganta está muito vermelha. Você está com uma infecção.
lines.en: Open your mouth and say ah. Your throat is very red. You have an infection.
lines.literal: Open the mouth and say ah. The throat is very red. You are with an infection.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Preciso tomar remédio?
lines.en: Do I need to take medicine?
lines.literal: I-need to-take medicine?

lines.speaker: Márcia
lines.pt: Vou passar um antibiótico. Tome um comprimido de oito em oito horas por sete dias.
lines.en: I will prescribe an antibiotic. Take one pill every eight hours for seven days.
lines.literal: I-go to-pass an antibiotic. Take a pill of eight in eight hours for seven days.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Posso trabalhar?
lines.en: Can I work?

lines.speaker: Márcia
lines.pt: Não. Descanse, beba bastante água e não tome nada frio. Vou te dar um atestado de três dias.
lines.en: No. Rest, drink plenty of water and do not have anything cold. I will give you a three-day note.
lines.literal: No. Rest, drink enough water and not take nothing cold. I-go you to-give a certificate of three days.

dialogues.title: At the pharmacy
dialogues.context: Carlos has a headache and a stuffy nose and asks the pharmacist Lúcia for advice.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Boa tarde! Posso ajudar?
lines.en: Good afternoon! May I help?

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Boa tarde. Estou com dor de cabeça desde ontem e o nariz está entupido. O que você recomenda?
lines.en: Good afternoon. I have had a headache since yesterday and my nose is stuffy. What do you recommend?
lines.literal: Good afternoon. I-am with pain of head since yesterday and the nose is stuffed. What you recommend?

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Você está com febre?
lines.en: Do you have a fever?
lines.literal: You are with fever?

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Não, só estou um pouco cansado. Acho que é um resfriado.
lines.en: No, I am just a little tired. I think it is a cold.
lines.literal: No, only I-am a little tired. I-find that it-is a cold.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Então leve este remédio pra gripe. Tome um comprimido de seis em seis horas.
lines.en: Then take this flu medicine. Take one pill every six hours.
lines.literal: Then take this medicine for flu. Take a pill of six in six hours.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Preciso de receita?
lines.en: Do I need a prescription?
lines.literal: I-need of prescription?

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Não precisa. Mas, depois de três dias, procure um médico.
lines.en: You do not need to. But after three days, see a doctor.
lines.literal: Not needs. But, after of three days, look-for a doctor.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: E pra tosse? Minha tosse também não passa.
lines.en: And for the cough? My cough will not go away either.
lines.literal: And for cough? My cough also not passes.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Leve também um xarope. E beba bastante água e não saia no frio.
lines.en: Take a syrup too. And drink plenty of water and do not go out in the cold.
lines.literal: Take also a syrup. And drink enough water and not go-out in-the cold.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Tá bom. Posso pagar com cartão?
lines.en: Okay. Can I pay by card?
lines.literal: Is good. Can I pay with card?

dialogues.title: A twisted foot
dialogues.context: Igor notices that his friend Rafaela is limping after a workout.

lines.speaker: Igor
lines.pt: Rafa, você está mancando. O que aconteceu?
lines.en: Rafa, you are limping. What happened?

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.pt: Torci o pé no treino ontem. Agora o pé dói, e o joelho também.
lines.en: I twisted my foot at practice yesterday. Now my foot hurts, and my knee too.
lines.literal: I-twisted the foot in-the practice yesterday. Now the foot hurts, and the knee also.

lines.speaker: Igor
lines.pt: Você foi ao médico?
lines.en: Did you go to the doctor?
lines.literal: You went to-the doctor?

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.pt: Fui ao posto de saúde hoje cedo. Esperei duas horas, mas o médico foi ótimo.
lines.en: I went to the health clinic early this morning. I waited two hours, but the doctor was great.
lines.literal: I-went to-the post of health today early. I-waited two hours, but the doctor was great.

lines.speaker: Igor
lines.pt: O que ele disse?
lines.en: What did he say?

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.pt: Disse que eu não devo correr por duas semanas. Tenho que fazer repouso e pôr gelo no pé três vezes por dia.
lines.en: He said I should not run for two weeks. I have to rest and put ice on my foot three times a day.
lines.literal: He-said that I not owe to-run for two weeks. I-have that to-make rest and to-put ice on-the foot three times per day.

lines.speaker: Igor
lines.pt: Então não treine amanhã, hein?
lines.en: Then do not work out tomorrow, okay?
lines.literal: Then not train tomorrow, huh?

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.pt: Pode deixar. Vou só assistir a séries e descansar.
lines.en: Will do. I am just going to watch shows and rest.
lines.literal: Can leave. I-go only to-assist to series and to-rest.

lines.speaker: Igor
lines.pt: Quer uma sopa? Eu levo pra você.
lines.en: Do you want some soup? I will bring it to you.
lines.literal: Want a soup? I take for you.

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.pt: Quero! Obrigada.
lines.en: Yes, please! Thank you.
lines.literal: I-want! Obliged.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the words of health and the body
grammar.explanation:
Every word in this lesson can be read and written with the rules from the first three lessons. Nothing here is an exception; the words are only new combinations. The method is the same each time. Divide the word into syllables, find the stressed one, read the default from the ending (a word ending in a, e or o, with or without a final s, or in am, em or ens, is stressed on the second to last syllable, and a word ending in anything else is stressed on the last), and write an accent only when the word breaks that default. The kind of accent then tells you about the vowel: the acute marks the stress and, on a, e or o, an open vowel, the circumflex marks the stress and a closed vowel, the tilde marks a nasal vowel, and the cedilla writes the s sound where c alone would be k.

Stress and accents. A word stressed on the third to last syllable is called a proparoxytone. No ending predicts that stress, so such a word always has an accent: médico, remédio, antibiótico, séries, ótimo, estômago, farmácia, and the único of Sistema Único de Saúde. In remédio, séries and farmácia the endings io, ies and ia count as two syllables (re-MÉ-di-o, far-MÁ-ci-a), so the stressed vowel really is third from the end. Names follow the same rule: Márcia and Lúcia are written with an accent for the reason farmácia is. Água is the same case: the ending ua also counts as two syllables for the accent rule (Á-gu-a), even though it is said in two beats, Á-gwa. Estômago shows the circumflex doing its usual job: the closed o of the stressed syllable, es-TÔ-ma-gu. Compare frio: its stressed vowel is the i, second from the end, exactly as the ending o predicts, so it needs no accent. A stressed one-syllable word ending in a, e or o takes an accent: pé, já, chá. The accent in saúde is a hiatus accent (a hiatus is two vowels in separate syllables): without it, au would be read as one syllable, as in aula, and with it the u stands alone, sa-Ú-de. Finally, the acute in dói marks the open o inside a stressed diphthong, for the same reason as the éi of papéis. Compare boi (ox), whose o is closed and which has no accent. The 2009 spelling agreement removed this accent only from words not stressed on their last syllable, such as ideia, so dói keeps it.

Nasal vowels. The tilde on mão, infecção, então and cartão marks a nasal vowel and, because no other accent is present, also the stress. The ending ão is a nasal diphthong, one syllable, said like ow through the nose. The plural of mão is mãos; the three plural endings of words in ão (ões, ães, ãos) cannot be predicted from the spelling, and mão is one of the words to learn. Elsewhere nasality is written with m or n before a consonant: dente, garganta, comprimido, descansar. The m or n is not a separate consonant sound there; it only nasalizes the vowel.

Consonants. C before a, o or u is the k sound and before e or i it is s, and the cedilla writes s where c alone would be k. So boca is BO-ka, cabeça is ca-BE-sa and receita is re-SEI-ta. Pescoço contains both: the c before o is k and the ç before o is s. In infecção, the first c closes a syllable and is k, and the ç before ã is s. A single s between vowels is z and ss writes the s sound: tosse is TÓ-si and repouso is re-POU-zu. G is the hard g before a, o, u and before r (garganta, gripe, diga) and the zh sound before e or i (gelo); j is always zh (joelho, hoje). Qu keeps the k sound before e (fique) and gu before a is pronounced gw (água). X at the start of a word is sh (xarope). The lh is one sound like the lli of million (olho, orelha, vermelho), the h is silent (hoje, horas, hein, ah), and rr is the strong r (barriga, socorro).

Sounds the spelling does not show. A final unstressed e is said i, and in most of Brazil a t or d before an i sound (a written i or that final e) is said ch or j: dente is DEN-chi and médico is MÉ-ji-cu. A final unstressed o is said u. An l that closes a syllable is said w: consulta is con-SUW-ta and mal is maw. The quality of an e or o without an accent, open or closed, is not written: febre has an open e and cabeça a closed one, so learn it with the word. It can even change in the plural: o olho has a closed o and os olhos an open one.

examples.en: The doctor gave me a prescription.
examples.literal: The doctor me gave a prescription.

examples.pt: Minha cabeça e meu pescoço doem.
examples.en: My head and my neck hurt.

examples.pt: Preciso de água e de repouso.
examples.en: I need water and rest.
examples.literal: I-need of water and of rest.

grammar.title: Pain and symptoms: doer, estar com and how long
grammar.explanation:
English reports pain by making a person the owner of a symptom: 'my head hurts', 'I have a headache', 'I have a fever'. Portuguese has two separate structures for the same job, and each has its own logic. The first uses the verb doer, 'to hurt', and the second uses estar com, 'to be with'.

Start with doer. A verb agrees with its subject, the thing that performs the action or is described by the verb, so the verb takes the ending that matches the subject's number. The subject of doer is the body part, not the person: a cabeça dói, os pés doem. The person does not hurt; the foot does. That is why doer appears almost only in two forms, dói for one thing and doem for more than one. The verb very often comes before its subject, as in Dói a cabeça and Doem os pés, and the order A cabeça dói is just as correct. Two things make the verb plural: Minha cabeça e meu pescoço doem. The acute on dói is explained in the spelling note; in doem the o and e are two separate syllables, do-em, so the stress stays on do.

The person who feels the pain can be shown with a small pronoun. An object is a person or thing that an action affects. A direct object receives the action itself (the doctor examines me), and an indirect object is the person to whom or for whom something happens (the doctor gives a note to me). In Me dói a cabeça, me means 'to me', so the sentence says literally 'to-me hurts the head'. The small pronoun stands before the verb, as the reflexive pronouns of the daily-routine lesson did. This form is correct, but in everyday speech most people prefer a possessive: Minha cabeça dói, or Dói o meu joelho. The full system of object pronouns comes in a later unit; for now you only need to recognize me, 'to me', and te, 'to you'.

To say that the pain is going on at this moment, use estar plus the gerund, as you did in the past with estava falando. The gerund is the -ndo form of the verb (-ando, -endo, -indo), and for doer it is doendo: A minha garganta está doendo. The plain present (dói) states a general fact or a pattern, 'my knee hurts whenever I climb stairs'. The progressive (está doendo) describes what is happening now, and it is the usual answer to Onde dói? English draws the same line between 'hurts' and 'is hurting'.

The second structure is estar com plus a noun. English treats a symptom as something you have. Portuguese treats it as something that is with you at the moment: Estou com febre is literally 'I am with fever', built like estou com fome and estou com sono in the feelings lesson. It uses estar because a symptom is a temporary condition, and com because the symptom accompanies you. Ter also works (Tenho febre), but estar com is the default. For an illness named by an adjective use estar plus the adjective: Estou gripado, where the ending -ado turns the noun gripe into an adjective. Ficar, 'to stay', describes the change into that state (Fiquei gripado, 'I ended up flu-ed'), and estar describes the state itself.

Two patterns follow the word dor. Dor de plus the organ is a set name for a kind of ache, just as English makes one compound of 'headache': dor de cabeça, dor de garganta, dor de dente, dor de ouvido, dor de barriga. Dor plus em, contracted with the article into no, na, nos or nas, says where the pain is: dor no peito, dor nas costas, dor no joelho. Dor is feminine, so the quantity word agrees: muita dor. By contrast muito stays unchanged before an adjective: muito vermelha. When a body part comes with an adjective, Portuguese uses the article where English uses 'my': Estou com o nariz entupido, literally 'I am with the nose stuffed'.

Finally, how long. English uses a special form, the present perfect, for a condition that began in the past and continues: 'I have had a fever since yesterday', 'for three days'. Portuguese does not need it, because the condition is still true now, so it uses the ordinary present: Estou com febre desde ontem. Desde names the starting point (desde ontem, desde segunda) and means 'since'. Há names the length of time (há três dias) and means 'for'. Há is literally 'there is' or 'it has', from the verb haver. With a past verb the same word means 'ago' (Comecei há três dias, 'I began three days ago'), which the past-time lesson introduced. Faz does the same job as há: faz três dias.

grammar.title: Advice: precisar, ter que, dever and é melhor
grammar.explanation:
Advice has a simple structure in Portuguese: a conjugated verb says how strong the advice is, and an infinitive says what to do. A verb that says whether an action is necessary, possible or permitted, instead of describing an action itself, is called a modal verb. You already know poder and querer; this note looks closely at three more, precisar, dever and ter que. The helper verb changes with the person (eu preciso, nós precisamos, eles precisam), and the infinitive after it never changes. English works with special words (must, should, need to, have to); Portuguese uses ordinary verbs with ordinary endings.

There are three levels of strength. Dever means 'should' or 'ought to' and is the gentlest, a recommendation. Its literal meaning is 'to owe', which explains it: what you owe is what is due from you. The same verb still means 'to owe' money (Eu devo cem reais ao médico) and, in another use, 'probably' (Ele deve estar em casa, 'he must be at home'). Precisar means 'to need': it says that something is necessary for your goal, and it is the friendly, everyday way to advise: Você precisa descansar. Ter que, literally 'to have that', means 'to have to': an obligation that comes from outside you. The que is the same linking word that you see in Acho que é um resfriado. Ter que is very frequent in speech and is often used with no stated subject: Tem que tomar esse remédio, 'one has to take this medicine'. In writing you also see ter de with the same meaning. The forms are tenho que, tem que, temos que and têm que, with the circumflex that marks the plural in writing.

The negatives do not just flip the meaning, and this is the trap for English speakers. English 'must not' means forbidden, while 'do not have to' means not required, and Portuguese keeps those ideas apart with different verbs. Você não deve correr is 'you should not run', advice against. Você não precisa correr is 'you do not need to run': it is not necessary. Você não tem que correr is 'you do not have to run': you are not obliged. For a real prohibition or 'you cannot', use poder: Você não pode correr. A short answer can repeat the verb alone: Preciso de receita? Não precisa.

É melhor plus the infinitive, literally 'is better to', is impersonal: nobody is the subject of é, so the sentence does not change with the person. É melhor ficar em casa is good for any listener. Precisar has one more rule about the little word de. Before a noun it takes de, 'to need of something': preciso de receita, preciso de um remédio. Before an infinitive it takes nothing: preciso descansar.

grammar.title: The imperative for advice: tome, não coma
grammar.explanation:
A command, a piece of advice or an instruction is given in the imperative mood. A mood, as the grammar map explained, is the attitude of the sentence: the indicative states facts and the imperative gives orders. English uses the bare verb ('take!'), but Portuguese has forms of its own. The command for você is what doctors, pharmacists, teachers and friends use, and it is not rude: a doctor who says Abra a boca sounds as neutral as English 'open your mouth'. Por favor makes it softer, and so does a question with poder: Pode abrir a boca?

The rule from the lesson on directions applies unchanged. Take the eu form of the present, drop the final -o, and add the opposite vowel: verbs in -ar take -e, and verbs in -er and -ir take -a. The vowel is opposite so that the command cannot be mistaken for a statement: você toma is a statement, and tome is an order. These forms are really borrowed from the present subjunctive, a mood taught at the intermediate level, so treat the pattern as a rule for now. Starting from the eu form is what makes the rule work for irregular verbs, because that form carries the irregularity with it: fazer has faço, so faça; dizer has digo, so diga; pôr has ponho, so ponha; sair has saio, so saia; dormir has durmo, with u for o, so durma. The sound must stay the same when the vowel changes, so the spelling adjusts: ficar gives fique (qu keeps the k before e), pagar gives pague (gu keeps the hard g), and começar gives comece (c before e is already s, so the ç is not needed). A few verbs do not follow from the eu form: ser gives seja, ir gives vá, estar gives esteja.

To forbid something, put não before the same form: Não tome, Não coma. The word nada, 'nothing', goes after the verb, and the não stays before it, because Portuguese uses negative concord, described in the lesson on frequency adverbs: Não coma nada frio is literally 'not eat nothing cold'. To speak to several people, add -m: tomem, comam, abram, descansem.

In casual speech Brazilians often give an order in the plain present instead: Toma esse remédio, Bebe água. This is the ordinary você form of the present, and it sounds more familiar and friendly, which is what you hear from friends and family. The forms in -e and -a are what professionals use and what you should write. As with other small pronouns in speech, me and te stand before the verb: Me liga! means 'call me!'.

Two phrases that belong to giving a dose. De oito em oito horas, literally 'of eight in eight hours', means every eight hours; it marks a regular interval, so de seis em seis horas is every six hours. Três vezes por dia, literally 'three times per day', gives the frequency.

grammar.title: Body parts, articles and reflexive verbs
grammar.explanation:
A possessive word (my, your, his) says who owns something. English uses it with body parts almost without exception: 'I broke my leg', 'wash your hands'. Portuguese uses the definite article instead whenever the owner is already clear from the sentence. Quebrei a perna is literally 'I broke the leg', and the only leg the speaker could have broken is their own. Lave as mãos is literally 'wash the hands'. The idea is economy: the subject of the verb already says whose body it is, so a possessive would say the same thing twice. English cannot do this because 'the leg' sounds like somebody's leg in general.

A possessive is still right when the owner is not clear or is being stressed. If someone else acts on your body, it is needed: A médica examinou a minha garganta, because the doctor is the subject and the throat could otherwise be hers. It is also used to contrast owners (Dói o meu joelho, não o seu) and when the body part is itself the subject: A minha cabeça está doendo. In speech the possessive usually comes with an article in front, as the family lesson showed.

The second principle is the reflexive verb. A reflexive verb has the same person as the one who acts and the one who receives the action, and it carries a small pronoun before the verb in Brazilian speech: Ele se cortou, 'he cut himself'. If you name the body part, the article does the job of showing ownership and the reflexive pronoun is usually dropped: Cortei o dedo rather than Eu me cortei o dedo. Both Eu me cortei and Cortei o dedo are natural. When somebody else acts on you, the small pronoun stands for the person who receives the action: O médico me examinou, 'the doctor examined me'. Vou te dar um atestado is 'I am going to give you a note', where te means 'to you' and sits between the two verbs. These pronouns are taught fully in a later unit.

The gerund can also stand alone, without estar. Cortei o dedo cozinhando means 'I cut my finger while cooking': the gerund says what the subject was doing at the same time as the main verb, and it never changes for person. English does the same with '-ing'.

Three details about the words themselves. A mão is feminine although it ends in o, so the article is a and the plural is as mãos. O pé becomes os pés. As costas has no singular, so the plural article is used even for one person's back. Finally, choose the verb for the situation: ficar for a change into a state (Fiquei gripado), estar for the current state (Estou cansado), doer for pain.

culture.title: SUS, planos de saúde and the farmácia
culture.text:
Brazil has one of the largest public health systems in the world, the SUS (Sistema Único de Saúde). It is free for everyone, including foreigners, and covers everything from vaccines and routine appointments at the posto de saúde to emergency care and complex surgeries. Many people also pay for a plano de saúde, a private insurance which usually gives faster access to specialists. For urgent cases there are UPAs, open 24 hours, and the pronto-socorro of hospitals. The emergency number for an ambulance is 192 (SAMU), and 193 is the fire department.

The farmácia plays a bigger role than in many countries. Pharmacists often recommend medicine for simple problems such as headache, cold or stomach upset, and most farmácias also apply injections and measure blood pressure. Antibiotics, however, require a receita. Big chains are open until late and some are open 24 hours, and many delivery apps bring medicine to your home. Generic medicines, called genéricos, are usually much cheaper than name brands.

Home remedies are also part of the culture. People drink chá de erva-doce, chá de camomila or chá de boldo for stomach ailments, and honey with lemon for a sore throat. If you are sick, you are likely to hear Melhoras!, literally 'improvements', meaning get well soon, or Se cuida!, literally 'yourself look-after', meaning take care. Both are friendly wishes, not formulas to answer with a long explanation; a simple Obrigado is enough. The vaccination campaigns of the SUS have a famous mascot, Zé Gotinha, a little drop with a smiling face that children know well.
